title: Amaziah: Right, but Not Wholeheartedly
summary: Amaziah punishes his father's murderers while sparing their sons, as the Law requires, and at a prophet's word he sends home the Israelite mercenaries he had hired. He defeats Edom, but then brings home the Edomites' gods and worships them, silences the prophet who rebukes him, and picks a needless fight with Jehoash king of Israel. Judah is routed, Jerusalem's wall is breached, the temple is plundered, and Amaziah eventually dies at the hands of conspirators.
story: Joash's reign ended with a murdered prophet and an assassinated king. His son Amaziah begins by setting things right, but the narrator's opening verdict hangs over everything that follows: he did right, "but not wholeheartedly" (verse 2). The chapter shows what a divided heart looks like in practice. Amaziah can obey a prophet when it costs money, yet he cannot resist the gods of a people he has just defeated. The kingdom of David is still standing, but the pattern of early faithfulness followed by pride and decline is becoming a habit in Judah's kings. His son Uzziah will repeat it in the next chapter.
historical:
Amaziah reigned in the early eighth century BC, commonly dated about 796 to 767 BC; because verse 25 says he lived fifteen years after Jehoash of Israel died, many historians think his son Uzziah began ruling alongside him for part of that time. The parallel is 2 Kings 14:1-20, which records the victory over Edom in the Valley of Salt, the capture of Sela (2 Kings 14:7), the war with Jehoash, and Amaziah's death at Lachish. Chronicles adds the hired Israelite troops, the two prophetic interventions, and Amaziah's worship of Edom's gods, and it explicitly ties his defeat and death to that apostasy.

The northern kingdom of Israel was then ruled by Jehoash (also spelled Joash), grandson of Jehu, whose dynasty had seized power a generation earlier. Edom, south and southeast of the Dead Sea, had rebelled against Judah in the days of Jehoram (2 Chronicles 21:8-10). Beth-shemesh, where the armies met, lay in the Sorek valley west of Jerusalem, and Lachish, where Amaziah fled, was Judah's major fortified city in the lowlands.
cultural:
Hiring soldiers was common practice in the ancient world, and a hundred talents of silver was a huge sum, roughly three tons or more by weight. The man of God's objection is not to mercenaries as such but to relying on Israel, whose northern kingdom had broken with the temple and David's line; the LORD, he says, "is not with Israel" (verse 7).

Amaziah's worship of Edom's gods looks senseless to a modern reader, but it followed an ancient logic. Conquerors often carried off the images of defeated peoples' gods, sometimes to display their victory and sometimes to win those gods' favor for themselves. The prophet exposes the absurdity in one question: why seek gods "which could not deliver them from your hand" (verse 15)? Jehoash's reply in verses 18-19 is a fable, a short animal-and-plant story used to mock a rival, much like Jotham's fable of the trees in Judges 9. A thistle proposing a marriage alliance to a cedar is ridiculous, and a passing beast ends the conversation.
literary: The chapter turns on counsel and hearing. The Hebrew root for advise appears three times around verses 16-17: Amaziah asks the prophet whether he has been made the king's "counselor", the prophet says the king has not heeded his "advice", and then Amaziah "took counsel" from others and challenged Israel. The man who will not listen to God's counsel finds other counsel that destroys him. The narrator also names the hidden cause in verse 20: Amaziah's refusal to listen "had come from God" because Judah had "sought the gods of Edom." The structure moves from obedience (verses 1-13) to idolatry (verses 14-16) to humiliation (verses 17-28), each stage a step down from the one before.

outline.t: Amaziah's reign and his just punishment of the assassins
The army mustered and the Israelite mercenaries dismissed
Victory over Edom and the raid by the dismissed troops
Amaziah worships Edom's gods and silences the prophet
War with Jehoash: defeat, the broken wall, the plundered temple
Amaziah's last years and death at Lachish

doctrines.note: Amaziah applies Deuteronomy 24:16, quoted in verse 4: each is to die for his own sin. Even in an age of blood feuds and dynastic purges, the Law set limits on vengeance and protected the children of the guilty.

The man of God tells Amaziah to walk away from a hundred talents with the promise that the LORD is able to give much more. Faith here is concrete: trusting God enough to accept a loss rather than rely on an alliance he has forbidden.
Amaziah's worship of gods that had just failed their own people shows idolatry as irrational as well as disloyal. It also shows that victory can be more spiritually dangerous than defeat.

words.note: Shalem, complete or whole. Verse 2 says Amaziah did right, but not with a whole heart. The same word describes the undivided heart David prayed for in Solomon (1 Chronicles 29:19). In Chronicles, a whole heart is the difference between occasional obedience and a life turned toward God.

Darash, to seek. It is one of the Chronicler's key words, usually for seeking the LORD in worship and prayer. Here it is turned against Amaziah: he has sought the gods of Edom (verses 15 and 20). The verb that should describe faithfulness now describes betrayal.
Yaats, to advise or take counsel. Its repetition in verses 16-17 links the prophet's rejected counsel with the reckless counsel Amaziah takes instead, the hinge between his idolatry and his downfall.

christ: Amaziah is a portrait of a divided king: right in outward actions, but with a heart that could be drawn after other gods and inflated by success. The whole line of David's sons in Chronicles leaves the reader longing for a king whose heart is entirely given to God, and the New Testament presents Jesus as that king. He resisted the offer of all the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship (Matthew 4:8-10), which is exactly the trade Amaziah made after his victory. The link is thematic rather than predictive: Amaziah's failure sharpens the hope for a son of David who would do what is right in the eyes of the LORD with his whole heart.

hard.q: How should a reader understand the throwing of ten thousand captives from a cliff in verse 12?
hard.a: The text reports this atrocity without praise; nothing says God commanded it, and the chapter immediately goes on to condemn Amaziah for what he did after the battle. Chronicles often records the brutal conduct of war in the ancient Near East, where killing prisoners was common, without endorsing it. Some readers see the act as part of the narrator's portrait of a king whose success was already corrupting him. Others note that large numbers in Chronicles may be stylized or represent military units rather than exact counts, a debated point. Either way, the chapter's verdict falls on the king's pride and idolatry, and the reader is not invited to celebrate the slaughter.

questions: The prophet told Amaziah that the LORD could give him much more than the hundred talents he would lose. When has obedience cost you something you had already paid for?
Amaziah worshiped the gods of the people he had just defeated. What do you tend to trust precisely after you have succeeded?
Amaziah asked the prophet, in effect, who made you my counselor? Whose correction do you resist most, and why?
